opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a great question, and it's something I think about a lot. A lot of the current work focuses on getting models to *execute* algorithms we already know: we give them examples of addition or sorting, maybe spell out the steps in the prompt, and see whether they can follow along and generalize to longer inputs. That's useful, and it tells us a lot about what these models can and can't represent. But executing an algorithm you've been shown is quite different from discovering one.

One thing that's missing is a good notion of what makes a solution *algorithmic* in the first place. When humans discover an algorithm, we're looking for something compact, reusable, something that works no matter how big the input gets. Language models are trained to predict the next token, so they're very happy to find shortcuts or heuristics that work on the training distribution but don't actually capture the underlying procedure. You see this in length generalization: the model looks like it's learned addition, and then you give it a slightly longer number and it falls apart. So I think we need inductive biases, or training signals, that push the model toward simple, general solutions rather than just whatever fits the data.

The second piece is the interaction loop. Discovery usually isn't a single forward pass. It's trying something, checking whether it works, noticing where it breaks, and revising. Models can do bits of this when you give them tools or a verifier, but we don't yet have a principled way of letting them build up abstractions over time, so that a subroutine they figured out in one problem becomes a building block they reliably reuse in the next.

And then there's evaluation. It's actually hard to tell whether a model has discovered something versus retrieved something it saw on the internet. If we want to make real progress here, we need settings where we can control what the model has been exposed to, so that when it comes up with a procedure we can be confident it's genuinely new to the model, and we can study *how* it got there. To me, that understanding of the process is just as interesting as the end result.

r001.rationale: The response calls for inductive biases or training signals and describes iterative testing, but does not suggest that fine-tuning is probably necessary to enable hypothesis generation.

r002.rationale: The response describes trying and checking solutions, but does not distinguish that process from aggregating candidates by majority vote or ensembling.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the thing that's most missing is that we tend to treat algorithm discovery as a one-shot generation problem, when really it's an iterative search problem that needs a good feedback loop.

Right now, the dominant paradigm is: you prompt the model, it writes some code or proposes some procedure, and you check whether it works. If it doesn't, you maybe try again with a slightly different prompt. But that's not how humans discover algorithms. We form a hypothesis, we test it on small cases, we notice where it breaks, we build intuition about why it breaks, and that intuition feeds the next hypothesis. The model needs to be in that loop, with the ability to run experiments, observe outcomes, and update its own beliefs about the problem structure.

The second thing I'd point to is that we don't give models good ways to represent what they've already learned about a problem. When a model is searching over a space of possible algorithms, it should be building up some kind of structured understanding, like "approaches of type A fail because of this property of the input, approaches of type B are promising but too slow." Instead, most systems either throw that context away between attempts, or stuff everything into an ever-growing prompt that gets noisier and noisier.

And then there's the question of what we're even optimizing for. A lot of the benchmarks reward getting the right answer on test cases, but discovering an algorithm is really about discovering the right abstraction. If the model finds a clever trick that happens to work on the test distribution but doesn't capture the underlying structure, we've learned very little, and the model hasn't either. I'd like to see more work where the signal comes from things like generalization to harder instances, or the ability to explain why the algorithm works, rather than just pass/fail on a fixed set.

So in short: more emphasis on iterative experimentation, better memory and representation of what's been tried, and evaluation that rewards understanding rather than just correctness on a narrow slice.

r001.rationale: The response describes iterative hypothesis generation and testing, but does not suggest that fine-tuning is necessary.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts one-shot generation with iterative experimentation, but does not distinguish hypothesis testing from majority voting or ensembling candidate solutions.

astra-6.text:
I think one thing that’s missing is a distinction between producing a program that works and discovering an algorithm. A model can write code that passes a set of tests, but that doesn’t necessarily tell us whether it’s found a general solution or pieced together patterns that happen to work on those examples.

So I’d like to see more emphasis on the process of discovery: can the model formulate a hypothesis, test it, find a counterexample, and use that counterexample to revise its approach? And then, can it explain why the resulting algorithm works and how its computational cost scales?

That also changes how we evaluate these systems. If we want to claim algorithm discovery, we need to test beyond the cases that guided the search—larger inputs, different structures, cases designed to expose a flawed assumption. Otherwise, it’s very easy to mistake success on a benchmark for finding something genuinely general.

r001.rationale: The response advocates hypothesis formation and testing, but does not say fine-tuning is probably necessary to enable hypothesis generation.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes algorithm discovery from writing code that passes tests, but does not contrast majority voting or ensembling candidate solutions with generating and testing hypotheses.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one thing that’s missing is a good feedback loop between proposing an algorithm and actually testing it. A language model can generate something that looks like an algorithm, or explain why it ought to work, but that’s different from discovering a procedure that’s correct and useful.

You want to give it a way to execute its ideas, find counterexamples, and revise them. And the evaluation has to distinguish between solving the examples you’ve shown it and finding something that generalizes—to larger inputs, to different distributions, or to cases where the familiar approach breaks down.

There’s also a question of what we’re asking it to discover. If the task is too close to existing textbook problems, it’s hard to tell whether you’re seeing discovery or a recombination of things it’s already encountered. I’d like to see more settings where there’s room for a genuinely different solution and where we can measure why that solution is better.

r001.rationale: The response calls for generating and testing algorithms but does not suggest that fine-tuning is probably necessary to enable hypothesis generation.
